title: Sorting Algorithms
notes: Long lecture (five pages, four algorithms plus a lower bound). Tests that a long source does not lose the later algorithms and keeps stability claims per algorithm. Traps: radix/counting sort, timsort and heap sort, which are not in this lecture.

pages.text:
Week 5 — Sorting.

A sort is stable if equal keys keep their original relative order. Stability matters when sorting by one field after another.

Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix: take the next element and shift larger ones right to insert it. Worst case O(n^2) (reverse-sorted input), best case O(n) (already sorted), O(1) extra space, stable. It is fast on small or nearly sorted inputs.
Merge sort splits the array in half, sorts each half recursively and merges the two sorted halves. Always O(n log n). It needs O(n) extra space for the merge. Stable.

Quicksort picks a pivot, partitions into smaller and larger elements, and recurses on both sides. Average O(n log n), but worst case O(n^2) when the pivot is repeatedly the smallest or largest, as with a sorted array and a first-element pivot. In place, not stable. Choosing a random pivot makes the worst case unlikely.
Any sort that works only by comparing elements needs at least on the order of n log n comparisons in the worst case. So merge sort is asymptotically optimal among comparison sorts.
